section: 1. Identify the most-recent date tag among saved CSVs
grain_in: one CSV file on disk in results/
operation: Lists results/ for files named as one of nine hard-coded bases followed by an ISO date and .csv, then sorts and keeps a single file per base; the tibble construction and the base/date parsing are absorbed because they only split the filename apart so the sort and the slice can act on it. The redundant second filter on base %in% base_names is absorbed as a no-op given the regex.
settings: nine base names listed in base_names; regex requires the suffix _YYYY-MM-DD.csv; ordering is arrange(base, desc(date), desc(fname)) with slice_head(n = 1), so a date tie is broken by the lexicographically largest filename; results_dir is fixed at script_dir/results.
na_behavior: date is NA only if no date substring is present, which the regex prevents, so an NA date cannot reach the sort. A base with no matching file yields no row at all; the only signal is the non-fatal warning in the block immediately below (missing_bases), after which the object is simply absent and the failure surfaces later as an object-not-found error at the rename step.

section: 2. Read each latest file into a named list
grain_out: named list, one element per base, each element a table at its own native grain
units_out: mixed: indices, counts, ratios, depending on the file
operation: Reads each selected CSV with readr::read_csv and turns base/data into a named list; select and deframe are absorbed because they only reshape the result for list2env. This is the boundary at which the meaning of every downstream quantity is inherited from files this script does not produce.
settings: show_col_types = FALSE; column types are guessed by readr from its default sample of the first 1000 rows, so no type is pinned and a mostly-empty numeric column can be read as logical or character.
na_behavior: read_csv maps the default na strings (empty field, NA) to NA, so a value that was never computed, a value that was written as NA, and a value that failed to parse all arrive as the same NA and are not distinguishable downstream. Parse problems are never inspected via problems(), so they do not stop the script.

section: 1) Standardize columns & align turnover to I_C at the same (bay x period x season) stratum
grain_out: bay x period x season with finite turnover
units_in: Bray-Curtis dissimilarity index, plus a pair count and a mean number of months
units_out: Bray-Curtis dissimilarity index, plus a pair count and a mean number of months
operation: Renames bray_bc to turnover, keeps six columns, coerces season to character so it will join, then drops rows whose turnover is not finite, which changes the set of strata described; the transmute is absorbed as a rename and select, the filter is the node. What bray_bc summarises, that is, which set of month pairs within a stratum was averaged, is not visible in this script.
settings: turnover is defined as the bray_bc column, flagged in a comment as the updated column; the QC filter n_pairs >= 2 and mean_months_per_pair >= 3 is written but commented out, so no minimum sampling effort is imposed and a stratum resting on one pair carries the same weight as one resting on many.
na_behavior: is.finite removes NA, NaN, Inf and -Inf alike, so a stratum with no comparable pairs, one whose dissimilarity was undefined, and one that overflowed all leave by the same route and are not distinguishable afterwards. No count of dropped rows is retained or printed.

grain_out: bay x period x season with finite I_C
operation: Selects the four columns needed, coerces season to character to match beta_bray_std, and drops rows whose I_C is not finite; select and mutate are absorbed as reshape and type alignment, the filter is the node. How I_C was computed, and on what aggregation of biomass or counts, is not visible in this script.
settings: no threshold beyond the finiteness test; columns other than major_area, period, season and I_C are discarded, so any effort or sample-size column that might have been used to weight the model is dropped here.
na_behavior: is.finite removes NA, NaN and infinite values together, so an unsampled stratum and one whose variance was zero (giving an infinite invariability) are dropped identically and cannot be told apart later. No count of dropped rows is retained.

section: 2) Join turnover with I_C at the same stratum
grain_in: bay x period x season, in two separate tables
grain_out: bay x period x season present in both tables and with I_C > 0
units_out: invariability index, its base-10 logarithm, and the dissimilarity index on one row
operation: Inner-joins invariability to turnover on bay, period and season, keeps only strata with I_C > 0, and adds log10_Ic; the factor level assignment is absorbed as a reformat, though it is what fixes Fall as the model reference, and the stopifnot is absorbed as a guard on the joined result. The join is the point at which one row starts to mean a stratum observed in both pipelines, and unmatched strata are dropped without being counted.
settings: keys major_area, period, season; inner join, so unmatched rows on either side vanish; I_C > 0 required, commented as needed for log10; season levels set to Fall, Spring, Summer, Winter, which makes Fall the reference level for the model that follows; logarithm base 10.
na_behavior: rows dropped for failing I_C > 0 and rows dropped for having no partner in the other table leave by different mechanisms but look identical afterwards, since neither is counted. A season value outside the four listed levels becomes NA silently and is then dropped by lmer. stopifnot fires only when the join is empty, not when it is small, so a join that matched a handful of strata passes.

units_out: coefficients in log10 index per unit of turnover; variances in squared log10 index
operation: Fits a linear mixed model of log10(I_C) on turnover and season with a random intercept for bay, via lmerTest::lmer so that Satterthwaite degrees of freedom and p-values are attached to the summary.
settings: REML is the lme4 default and is not overridden; period appears neither as a fixed nor a random term although rows are one per bay x period x season, so repeated periods within a bay are treated as exchangeable replicates and any temporal trend is absorbed into the residual; turnover enters linearly and untransformed; rows are unweighted, so n_pairs and mean_months_per_pair carried through beta_bray_std are never used; random intercept only, no random slope on turnover.
na_behavior: na.action defaults to na.omit, so any row with a missing value in a model variable is dropped without notice, and the number of rows actually fitted is never printed or compared with nrow(df_turnover_ic). A singular fit or a convergence warning is a warning only and does not stop the script, so the coefficients that follow may come from a degenerate fit.

units_out: coefficients in log10 index per unit of turnover; variances in squared log10 index
operation: Fits the same specification without the season term, to serve as the reduced model in the likelihood-ratio test below. It is the same call on the same data as the previous node but with a different formula, so it is counted as a separate node.
settings: REML default, same as the full model; note that the anova() comparison below refits both models with maximum likelihood, so these REML fits are not the ones tested.
na_behavior: same silent na.omit as the full model. Because season is absent here, a row with a missing season would be kept in this fit and dropped from the full fit, which would make the two fits use different row sets; anova() would then error rather than return a wrong test, but nothing in the script checks it in advance.

units_out: deviance, a chi-square statistic, degrees of freedom, a p-value
operation: Compares the reduced and full models by likelihood-ratio test. anova.merMod refits both with maximum likelihood before comparing, so the test reported here is not computed from the REML fits whose summary is printed alongside it; the cat and print calls are absorbed because they only display results.
settings: refit = TRUE is the default and the ML refitting happens silently; the reduced model is given first, so the test is for adding season; three degrees of freedom for the three season contrasts.
na_behavior: anova stops with an error if the two fits used different numbers of observations, so this failure is loud rather than silent. No NA is produced. The p-value is not adjusted for the fact that the same data also produced the fixed-effect p-values printed below.

units_in: log10 index per unit of predictor
units_out: log10 index, standard error, t, p, plus a multiplicative factor on I_C and a percent change
operation: Extracts the fixed-effect table from the lmerTest summary and computes effect_mult = 10^estimate and effect_pct = (effect_mult - 1) * 100, which is arithmetic combining a model estimate with the log base chosen earlier; moving rownames into a column and relabelling the terms are absorbed as reshape and rename. For the turnover row the multiplier is the fold change in I_C per one unit of turnover, and since Bray-Curtis is bounded on 0 to 1 that unit spans the entire possible range of the predictor rather than a typical increment. For the intercept row the same arithmetic is applied to the fitted value at turnover = 0 in Fall, so the column labelled per cent change versus reference has no reference to compare against on that row.
settings: back-transform base 10, matching the log10 taken in the join node; per cent expressed relative to 1; terms recoded to Intercept (Fall), Spring, Summer and Winter with .default = term, so the turnover row keeps its original name; no confidence interval is computed or back-transformed, only the point estimate.
na_behavior: the df and Pr(>|t|) columns exist only because lmerTest is attached; if the fit had come from lme4 alone the transmute would fail with an object-not-found error rather than produce NA. Otherwise no NA arises, since 10^x is finite over any plausible estimate.

grain_out: one row per variance component: bay intercept and residual
units_out: a variance and a standard deviation in log10 index units
operation: Pulls the variance components out of the fitted model and assembles a two-row table with sd taken as the square root of the variance; components are picked by matching grp to major_area and to Residual and taking the first match, and the cat and print calls are absorbed as display only.
settings: rows selected by name with [1], so if VarCorr returned more than one row for a group the first is taken with no warning; sd is recomputed as sqrt(vcov) rather than read from the sdcor column VarCorr already provides; the label Random intercept (bay) assumes major_area is a bay, which the script never states.
na_behavior: if either grp label were absent the subset would return a zero-length vector and tibble would error on the length mismatch rather than fill NA, so this failure is loud. sqrt of a negative variance would give NaN with a warning, which a converged fit cannot produce but which nothing guards against.

section: 5) Figure: population-level lines by season (fixed effects only)
end_anchor: pred_grid$log10_Ic_hat <- predict(mod_season, newdata = pred_grid, re.form = NA)
grain_in: bay x period x season, plus one fitted model
grain_out: turnover grid point x season, 200 x 4 = 800 rows
operation: Builds an evenly spaced grid of 200 turnover values spanning the observed range, crossed with the four seasons, and attaches population-level fitted values with the random effects excluded; taking the range and reading the factor levels are absorbed because they only supply the grid bounds. One row stops meaning an observed stratum and starts meaning a hypothetical point on the fitted surface. The grid uses the pooled turnover range for every season, so lines are drawn across turnover values that were not observed within a given season or bay.
settings: length.out = 200; range taken over all rows pooled, with na.rm = TRUE; re.form = NA, so bay intercepts are excluded and the lines are population-level rather than bay-specific; season levels are read from the factor as ordered at this point, Fall Spring Summer Winter, and are reordered to Fall Winter Spring Summer further down for plotting only, after the model has already been fitted.
na_behavior: predict with re.form = NA returns a value for every grid row and cannot yield NA here, since the grid contains no missing values and no new factor level. na.rm = TRUE in range conceals the case where turnover is entirely missing, which would give an infinite range and a grid of non-finite values rather than an error.
